subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: reasoning that everyone does it [Pitfall]
passage:
On the bench outside the tea shop in the small town, after Class 10 tuition, Anand held up his phone. “Everyone's using AI for the essays. Half of 10-B. So it's fine.”
Ishita frowned. “Sir said the assignment has to be your own.”
“Sir doesn't know how many do it. If everybody does, that's basically the rule.” He liked that sentence and repeated it in his head all the way home. He pasted the prompt, submitted the answer and felt good. Then Ishita's essay, stumbling and honest, got 7 marks and his got 9 for no effort of his own, and he felt a small, unpleasant pinch. He shrugged it off. Later, when the teacher asked him to write two lines on the topic in class, he found he couldn't.

qa.q: What did Anand say about the rest of the class?
qa.a: Anand said everyone is using AI for the essays, half of 10-B.

qa.q: What might Anand's small pinch mean?
qa.a: Anand may feel uneasy and a little guilty, sensing it is not fair that his effortless answer beat Ishita's honest one.
Anand could follow the school's rule, use AI only to explain ideas and write the essay himself, since a crowd's habit does not change fairness or his own learning.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel about the marks?
qa.a: Ishita may feel frustrated or unfairly treated, since Ishita's honest work earned fewer marks than an answer with no effort.

grounding: A student argues that classmates already use AI for assignments, so it must be fine, and ignores school rules, fairness and his own skill development.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: reasoning that everyone does it [Pitfall]
passage: "Literally everyone uses it," Oskar said, sliding his laptop across the library table. "Emma's history essay? AI. Half of Year 11. If the whole class does it, it can't be cheating." Bilal looked at the screen, where a smooth, polished essay on the causes of the First World War sat under Oskar's name. "The school rules say you have to declare it." "Nobody declares it." Oskar submitted it that night. Two weeks later Ms. Hughes kept him back after class. His essay had been flagged, and she asked him to talk through his argument. He couldn't explain why he'd ranked the alliances above the arms race. The essay got a zero and a meeting with his parents. Walking home, Oskar muttered, "Everyone does it." Bilal said quietly, "Maybe. But everyone wasn't asked to explain."

qa.a: The causes of the First World War.

qa.q: Why did Oskar feel it was fine to submit the AI essay?
qa.a: Oskar felt safe and justified because so many classmates seemed to do it, which made him brush aside the rule about declaring it.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Oskar approached it?
qa.a: Check the school rule and write his own argument, using AI only to understand the topic, so he could explain every choice if asked.

qa.q: How might Bilal see Oskar's excuse on the walk home?
qa.a: Bilal seems unconvinced, pointing out that others doing it didn't help when Oskar alone had to explain his work.

grounding: Shows a student reasoning that classmates already use AI to write assignments, ignoring school rules and his own learning, and paying the price.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: reasoning that everyone does it [Pitfall]
passage: In the evening study hall of the residential school, Suraj had an AI tool open under his Hindi textbook. "It's writing my nibandh," he whispered to Anjali. "Relax. Everyone in our block does it. Ma'am can't check forty essays." Anjali frowned. "The notice board says graded work must be your own." "Rules are for show." He handed in the neat essay the next day and got nine out of ten. Three weeks later came the half-yearly exam: a nibandh on a similar topic, written by hand in the hall. Suraj stared at the blank page for ten minutes. He hadn't built a single Hindi paragraph himself all term. He wrote half a page. That evening, Anjali found him in the study hall with the textbook open, and no tool.

qa.q: What mark did the AI essay get?
qa.a: It got nine out of ten.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling as he stared at the exam page?
qa.a: Suraj was probably panicked and stuck, realising he had never practised building a Hindi paragraph himself.

qa.q: What else could Suraj have done during the term?
qa.a: Suraj could have written the essays himself and used the tool only to explain words or check grammar, following the notice-board rule.

qa.q: How might Anjali see Suraj in the study hall that evening?
qa.a: Anjali may feel a bit sorry for him but hopeful, seeing him finally working from the textbook without the tool.

grounding: Illustrates a student who uses AI for graded essays because everyone does, ignoring the rules, and then cannot write on his own in the exam.
